blocks.text: Dear Sandra:

Thank you for the long afternoon you and the shareholders spent with Richard Mccoy and me this month, and for being so plain with us about what the company wants new capital to do and what it is unwilling to give up in order to get it. This letter sets out the terms on which Quillon Harbor Advisors will act as financial advisor to {{fact:f:E-2022-001.client}} in raising growth capital, and we have put the commercial terms first so that you and the shareholders can settle them before turning to the work itself.
Fee and Start of the Engagement

Our fee for this engagement is {{fact:f:E-2022-001.fee}}. It covers the whole of the work this letter describes, from our first review of the company's figures through to the closing of a financing, and it will not increase if the raise asks more of our time than any of us now expects.

The engagement will begin on {{fact:f:E-2022-001.start}}, and we expect it to run for about five months from that day, which is the time a well-prepared raise usually needs to travel from first materials to signed documents. Should the calendar move for reasons on either side, we will tell you as soon as we see it coming, and the fee will stay where it is.
How We Will Approach the Raise

We will begin with the company and come to the market only once we understand it as an investor will. Justin Gonzalez, an Analyst in our Advisory group, will build the financial model alongside your team and set the company beside comparable growth financings, so that before any investor hears from us, you and the shareholders will have our considered view of the valuation the market is likely to support and of the terms that usually travel with it.

From that work we will prepare a short summary that describes the business by its sector and size without naming it, and a fuller confidential presentation for investors who have signed a confidentiality agreement. Kelly Brown, also an Analyst with us, will assemble a list of {{fact:f:E-2022-001.scope}} drawn from growth equity funds, family offices and other minority investors whose mandates suit a company of this kind, and you will approve that list name by name before a single call is placed.

Once outreach begins, Kelly will keep a written log of every contact and every reply, and we will report to you on it each week, so that you always know who has been approached and what each of them has said. Richard Mccoy, a Partner of the firm, will lead the engagement, make the introductions himself, and sit with you and the shareholders through every investor meeting and every discussion of terms.

Investors who wish to go further will meet management and then be given access to a data room that we will organize with your team. We will then gather their term sheets, set them side by side for you with our written view of each, and work with you and the company's counsel through the negotiation of the definitive documents and on to closing.

I will read every document before it leaves our office, and I will be available whenever a decision would benefit from a second voice on our side. In return we will ask a good deal of your team, chiefly timely access to the monthly results and to management, and we will keep our requests organized and as few as the work allows.
Invoicing and Expenses

Our invoices will be addressed to you, and each is payable on receipt. The company will also reimburse our reasonable out-of-pocket expenses, which in a raise of this kind are chiefly travel to investor meetings, and we will ask your approval before incurring any single expense that falls outside the ordinary course.
Ending the Engagement

This engagement continues until a financing closes or until either of us ends it by written notice to the other, which either of us may give at any time and for any reason. If the company ends the engagement and then, within the following year, completes a financing with an investor we introduced, the fee will remain payable, since that investor will have come to the company through our work.
Confidentiality

We will hold in confidence everything the company shares with us and will use it for this engagement alone. Nothing that leaves our office before an investor has signed a confidentiality agreement in a form you have approved will name the company, and the confidential presentation will go only to investors who have signed one. Neither of us will announce a financing, or describe our part in it publicly, without the other's consent.
Our Role

We act for the company alone in this matter, and we will accept no fee or other payment from any investor in connection with it. If we come to learn of a relationship between the firm and an investor on the list that you would want to know about, we will tell you before that investor is approached, and you may strike it from the list without any discussion.
Limitation of Liability

We will rely on the information the company and its advisers provide without verifying it independently, and we do not give legal, tax or accounting advice, for which the company should look to its own counsel and accountants. We will bring care and our best judgment to the work, but we cannot promise that any investor will commit or that a financing will close on particular terms, and our liability to the company arising from this engagement will not exceed the fees paid to us under this letter.
Governing Law

This letter is governed by the law of the state in which our principal office is located, and the courts of that state will hear any dispute that arises under it. It is the whole of our agreement on these matters and may be changed only by a writing that both of us sign.

If these terms match your understanding, please sign below on behalf of {{fact:f:E-2022-001.client}} and return a copy to me. When it arrives, Richard Mccoy will telephone you to arrange the first working session, where Justin Gonzalez and Kelly Brown will take your team through the information we will need in order to begin.

blocks.text: Five workstreams, four owners on our side, one counterpart at the company. The engagement opened on {{fact:f:E-2022-001.start}}, and this note records how the work for {{fact:f:E-2022-001.client}} is divided. It is written for Richard Mccoy, Justin Gonzalez and Kimberly Harris. Sandra Waters is our single counterpart at the company, and requests to her team go through Kimberly Harris.

The split follows the order in which an investor will test the company. (1) The numbers come first. The model and the valuation view sit with one person, Justin Gonzalez, and every figure in the presentation will be taken from his model and from nowhere else. (2) The list and the log sit with me. There will be one record of who was approached, when, by whom, and with what answer. The engagement letter scopes the list at {{fact:f:E-2022-001.scope}}, and I will build to that unless Richard Mccoy tells me otherwise after the first review. (3) Kimberly Harris takes the information request and the data room together. Both draw on the same documents from the finance team, and one person asking for them means fewer requests landing on Sandra Waters. (4) Richard Mccoy keeps the investor conversations, so that every investor hears one voice from us. (5) The presentation is split between narrative and drafting. Richard Mccoy decides what the company says about itself; Kimberly Harris turns that into pages and keeps the version history.

One dependency governs the order of everything else. No investor is contacted until two conditions hold: (a) the model ties to the July close and Richard Mccoy has signed off the valuation view; and (b) Sandra Waters has approved every name on the list on behalf of the company. The presentation cannot be finished before (a), because its financial pages come from the model. The list cannot be finished before the positioning is agreed, because which investors fit depends on what the company is raising money to do. The information request has nothing upstream of it. That is why it goes out first. If it comes back late, every other workstream moves by the same number of days.

Confidentiality applies from today, not from first calls. Until the list is approved, nothing leaves this office with the company's name on it. The anonymous summary describes the business by sector and revenue band only. Internal files use the client name, but drafts sent outside the team, including to the company's own advisers, go through Richard Mccoy first. The contact log will record the date each confidentiality agreement is signed, and the confidential presentation goes to no investor without one.

The information request goes to Sandra Waters on Wednesday, so three points need settling before then. (1) Richard, should family offices be called in the first round, or held for a second? (2) Justin, how far back do you want the monthly results to go? (3) Kimberly, should the data room open alongside the confidential presentation, or only after first calls? Answers by Tuesday evening, in writing if possible, so that I can fold them into the request.
Outreach Review: {{fact:f:E-2022-001.client}} Growth Capital Raise

Kelly Brown, Analyst, Quillon Harbor Advisors

blocks.text: The session opened with outreach. Kelly Brown reported that the first round is complete, and that the contact log closed at {{fact:f:E-2022-001.pipeline-investors-approached}} as of yesterday evening. Calls went first to the investors Sandra Waters ranked highest when she approved the list. Most have answered. Those that declined gave the usual reasons: a company outside their size range, or a portfolio company too close to this one. Several have asked for the confidential presentation, and each will receive it once its confidentiality agreement is signed.

Richard Mccoy summarized what investors asked on first calls. Three questions recurred. What is the capital for? Will the shareholders keep running the company? How much of the business rests on its largest customers? The presentation answers the first two. The third needs a page of its own, built from the customer data the company has already provided.

Sandra Waters then raised whether to add a strategic investor from the company's own industry. The group discussed it and dropped it. A strategic holder would see customer terms and pricing. The shareholders have said from the start that they want a financial partner. The list stays as approved.

Justin Gonzalez took the group through the August results, which are now in the model. Nothing in them moves the valuation range the shareholders saw before outreach began. He asked whether the presentation should also carry a downside case. Richard Mccoy advised against it, on the ground that investors build their own downside and judge the company on the base case. Justin's objection was fair: an investor left to build its own downside may build a harsher one than ours. The point was not pursued.

Nancy Burgess, who now keeps the data room index, reported on the data room. The index is built from the company's first deliveries. Two folders are thin: customer contracts and the lease schedule. Sandra Waters will have both filled before any investor is given access.

Kelly Brown asked whether investors that declined should be called again after the meetings. Richard Mccoy said no. A second call to a firm that has already said no reads as pressure, and it tells the market the process is short of interest. The point was dropped.

Kelly Brown then raised the timing of management meetings. Several investors would like to meet in the second half of October. Sandra Waters noted that her team closes the quarter in the same weeks. The group agreed to hold meetings to two days a week until the close is done. A suggestion to run the first meetings by video was raised and set aside; the shareholders want to meet investors in person.

Three matters were left open. The first is governance. Investors will ask what board representation and which consent rights the shareholders will accept from a minority holder, and we need an answer before the first meeting. Sandra Waters carries this to the shareholders. The second is the meeting calendar itself. Kelly Brown carries it, and she needs the quarter-close dates from Sandra Waters to finish it. The third is the customer page raised earlier, which is not yet drafted. Justin Gonzalez carries it and will circulate a draft to the team before it goes into the presentation.
Next step: Kelly Brown sends the draft meeting calendar to Sandra Waters on Tuesday.
Growth Capital Raise for {{fact:f:E-2022-001.client}}: Report at Mid-October
For Sandra Waters, Chief Financial Officer. From Kelly Brown, Analyst, with Richard Mccoy, Partner, and Justin Gonzalez, Analyst. Confidential to the company, its shareholders and its counsel.

This report covers the two weeks since our working session at the end of September, when the first round of outreach closed. The period opened with follow-up calls. Richard Mccoy spoke again with each investor that had asked for more, and in most cases the second call was about the shareholders' plans for the capital and their own role afterward. Justin Gonzalez answered the questions on the model that came back from those calls. Most concerned the August margin and the hiring assumptions in the plan. The confidential presentation went to each investor as its confidentiality agreement was signed. A small number declined after reading it, mostly on size, and none of them raised a concern about the business itself. Your team filled the customer contracts and lease schedule folders last week, so the data room is ready for the investors who go forward. I sent you the draft meeting calendar on the Tuesday after the session, and your quarter-close dates let us fix the meeting days around the close. By the end of the period the first management meetings were set for two days in the last week of October, within the limit agreed at the session. No investor has yet been given access to the data room.

What investors are telling us has been consistent. Three themes came up on most follow-up calls. The first is use of proceeds: investors want to see the capital tied to the specific hires and investments named in the plan. The second is the shareholders' roles after a raise. Investors are reassured that management stays, and several asked who would run the company day to day if a founder stepped back. The third is customer concentration, and it is the one we are least ready on. Justin Gonzalez is preparing a page on it from the contracts now in the data room, so that investors have the answer in front of them before the meetings. None of the three is new. All of them came up on first calls as well, which suggests investors are reading the presentation closely.

The figures for the period measure different things, so I give them one at a time. The approved investor list stands at {{fact:f:E-2022-001.scope}}; nothing has been added to it or removed from it since you approved it. The contact log closed the first round at {{fact:f:E-2022-001.pipeline-investors-approached}}, and it has not moved this period, because we have made no new first calls. The valuation view still rests on {{fact:f:E-2022-001.comparators}} that Justin Gonzalez assembled before outreach began; we have not changed the set. The fee is unchanged at {{fact:f:E-2022-001.fee}}, as the engagement letter set it, and expenses this period were negligible. I would treat the contact log figure as final for the first round. A second round would be opened only with your agreement, and I do not expect us to recommend one before the meetings have been held and we know which investors want to continue.

The next stage is diligence for the investors who want to go further after meeting management, and after that, term sheets. We expect the first investors to ask for data room access in November. That expectation rests on four assumptions. (1) The management meetings go ahead in the last week of October as set. (2) The shareholders settle their position on board representation and consent rights before those meetings, because investors will raise it in the room. (3) The September quarter closes in line with the plan, since every investor will set it beside the model. (4) Investors take longer to commit this autumn than they did a year ago, with rates rising as they have been, and we have built the calendar on that basis. If (2) slips, the meetings can still go ahead, but we would expect fewer investors to ask for diligence afterward.

One risk sits outside these assumptions. If the customer page does not settle the concentration question, investors may ask for customer calls before they commit to diligence. That would add time in November. We would want your view on whether any customer could be approached, and on what terms, before an investor asks.

Some of this depends on you, so I set out what we need before the first meetings. (1) The shareholders' position on governance, in writing, by the end of next week. (2) The September results as soon as the quarter is closed. (3) Confirmation that you and the shareholders can hold both meeting days in the last week of October. Richard Mccoy will call you on Tuesday to go through the meeting order, and I will send the next report once the first meetings are done.
